stem: What does a distributed trace record?

options.text: The path taken by a single request as it propagates through multiple services
options.note: Right. That's the primer's definition.

options.text: An aggregated error rate across all requests
options.note: That's a metric.

options.text: Every log line from one server
options.note: That's a log stream, not a trace.
That's a metric.

explanation: A distributed trace, more commonly called a trace, records the path taken by a single request as it propagates through multiple services.

options.text: A single unit of work or operation within a trace
options.note: Right. Spans are the building blocks of traces.

options.text: The total time range of a dashboard
options.note: Not in tracing terms.
That's Alertmanager grouping.
Spans are tracing data, not labels.

explanation: A span represents a single unit of work or operation. Spans track specific operations that a request makes.

stem: In a trace, what does the root span represent?

options.text: The request from start to finish; spans beneath it show the steps
options.note: Right. It's the first span and has no parent.

options.text: The slowest operation in the trace
options.note: The root isn't defined by speed.
A database call is usually a child span.
Root means the top of the hierarchy, not last in time.

explanation: A trace is made of one or more spans. The first span is the root span. Each root span represents a request from start to finish, and spans underneath give more detail.

stem: Which of these does a span include? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. It describes the operation.
Right. They show how long it took.
Right. For example http.route.
PromQL is Prometheus's query language. It isn't part of a span.

explanation: A span includes a name, parent span ID (empty for root spans), start and end timestamps, span context, attributes, span events, span links and span status.
hint: One option belongs to a different tool.

stem: How do tracing systems know which spans belong to the same trace?

options.text: All spans in a trace share the same trace ID in their span context, with parent IDs giving the hierarchy
options.note: Right. That's what makes separate spans one trace.

options.text: They were recorded on the same server
options.note: A trace spans many services and servers.
Spans in a trace usually have different names.

options.text: They occurred within the same minute
options.note: Timing alone can't connect spans reliably.

explanation: Span context contains the trace ID of the trace the span belongs to, plus the span's own ID. Spans sharing a trace_id, with parent_id hierarchy, form a trace.
hint: There's an identifier in the span context.

stem: What is context propagation in distributed tracing?

options.text: Passing span context (including the trace ID) between services, so their spans join the same trace
options.note: Right. It's the core concept that makes distributed tracing work.
That's remote write.
That's Alertmanager routing.
Unrelated.

explanation: Context propagation is the core concept that enables distributed tracing. It lets spans be correlated and assembled into a trace regardless of where they're generated.
hint: Something must travel with the request.

stem: A span completes without any error and the developer didn't set a status. What is its status?

options.text: Unset, which means it completed without an error
options.note: Right. Ok is only for spans explicitly marked successful.
Ok must be set explicitly. The default is Unset.
No error occurred.
Pending is an alert state, not a span status.

explanation: Span status is Unset, Error or Ok. The default is Unset, meaning the operation completed without error. Ok means a developer explicitly marked it successful.
hint: The default value is the answer.

stem: An outgoing HTTP request from your service to another service is typically which span kind?

options.note: Right. A synchronous outgoing remote call.
Server spans represent incoming calls.
Consumer spans process queued jobs.
Internal spans don't cross a process boundary.

explanation: A client span represents a synchronous outgoing remote call, such as an outgoing HTTP request or database call. A server span represents an incoming one.

stem: Which problem is distributed tracing especially good at solving?

options.text: Finding which service or step made one specific request slow in a distributed system
options.note: Right. Traces break down what happens within a request.
That's a metrics job.
Traces aren't a log store.
That's service discovery.

explanation: Distributed tracing lets you observe requests as they propagate through distributed systems. It makes finding the root cause of performance problems far less daunting.

stem: How can Prometheus metrics be linked to traces?

options.text: Through exemplars, which can attach a trace ID to a metric sample in the OpenMetrics format
options.note: Right. From a latency spike you can jump to an example trace.

options.text: Prometheus stores full traces alongside metrics
options.note: Prometheus doesn't store traces.

options.text: By adding a trace_id label to every series
options.note: That's unbounded cardinality.
/metrics serves metrics, not traces.

explanation: Using the OpenMetrics format allows exposing and querying exemplars. An exemplar is a point-in-time snapshot related to a metric, and may carry a trace ID for use with a tracing system.
hint: An OpenMetrics feature from the exposition format topic.
